questions.stem: What is scarcity in economics?
options: A shortage caused by poor planning
A temporary shortage caused by high demand
A rare product
Limited resources relative to unlimited wants
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic economic problem, and it is why choices must be made.

questions.stem: What is opportunity cost?
options: The cost of producing a good
A cost that cannot be avoided
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
The total money spent
questions.explanation: Every choice forgoes something. Opportunity cost names what was sacrificed.

questions.stem: What is demand?
options: The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price
The amount producers make
The total money in an economy
The cost of raw materials
questions.explanation: Demand links quantity to price, and requires both willingness and ability to pay.

questions.stem: What is supply?
options: The number of shops in an area
The price of a good
The quantity of a good producers are willing to offer at a given price
The amount consumers want
questions.explanation: Supply is the producer side of the market.

questions.stem: What generally happens to demand when the price of a good rises?
options: Demand stays exactly the same
Supply falls instead
Demand usually falls
Demand usually rises
questions.explanation: Higher prices generally discourage buying, all else being equal.

questions.stem: What generally happens to supply when the price of a good rises?
options: Demand rises too
Supply usually rises
Supply usually falls
Supply is unaffected
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more attractive, so more is offered.

questions.stem: What is a budget?
options: A plan for income and spending over a period
A record of past purchases only
A type of bank account
A government tax
questions.explanation: Budgets are forward-looking plans, which is what distinguishes them from a record of spending.
questions.teaching:
Managing money starts with planning, and the plan has a specific name.

It sets out expected income over a period and how that income will be allocated — fixed costs, variable costs, saving. Governments produce one annually, and so do households and businesses. Its value is that it makes trade-offs visible before the money is spent rather than after, which is what separates it from simply tracking where money went. A surplus means income exceeds planned spending; a deficit means the reverse.

questions.stem: What is income?
options: Money received, such as from wages, a business or investments
Money spent on goods
The value of things you own
Money borrowed from a bank
questions.explanation: Borrowed money is a liability, not income.

questions.stem: What is a wage?
options: A payment made to a business owner from profits
Money earned from investments
A government payment
Payment for work, usually calculated by hours worked
questions.explanation: Wages are usually hourly; salaries are a fixed annual amount.

questions.stem: What is profit?
options: The cost of running a business
The tax a business pays
Revenue remaining after costs are paid
The total money a business receives
questions.explanation: Total money received is revenue; profit is what is left after costs.

questions.stem: What is an entrepreneur?
options: Someone employed by a large company
A government official
Someone who only invests in shares
Someone who starts a business and takes on the associated risk
questions.explanation: Risk-taking and initiative are the defining features.

questions.stem: What is taxation?
options: Compulsory payments to government used to fund public services
Voluntary donations to charity
A fee paid to a business
Money borrowed by the government
questions.explanation: Tax revenue funds services such as health, education and infrastructure.

questions.stem: What is a consumer?
options: A person who buys goods or services for their own use
A person who produces goods
A business that sells goods
A government agency
questions.explanation: Consumers purchase; producers make.

questions.stem: What is a need compared with a want?
options: A need is what a person values most; a want is what they can afford
Needs are provided by government; wants are bought privately
A need is essential for survival; a want is desired but not essential
A need becomes a want once it has been satisfied
questions.explanation: Food and shelter are needs; a new phone is a want.

questions.stem: What is a scam?
options: A government tax
A dishonest scheme designed to take money or information
A legitimate sale
A type of budget
questions.explanation: Recognising scams is named in the curriculum as part of being a smart consumer.
questions.teaching:
Consumers face several kinds of risk, and this one involves deliberate deception.

The defining feature is dishonest intent: someone sets out to obtain money or personal information by misleading you, through a fake message, a false investment, a bogus prize or an impersonated organisation. That separates it from a bad deal, which may be poor value but is honestly described, and from a faulty product, which is a failure rather than a deception. Urgency and unexpected contact are the two most reliable warning signs.

questions.stem: What is a sole trader?
options: A business owned by shareholders
A partnership of two people
A government-owned business
A business owned and run by one person
questions.explanation: The sole trader owns the business personally and bears full responsibility for it.

questions.stem: What is a partnership in business?
options: A company listed on the stock exchange
A charity
A business owned by two or more people who share profits and responsibility
A business with only one owner
questions.explanation: Partners share both the returns and the liabilities.

questions.stem: What is a company?
options: A business owned by one person
Any group of workers
A government department
A business that is a separate legal entity from its owners
questions.explanation: Separate legal identity is what limits owners' personal liability.

questions.stem: What does 'consumer sovereignty' mean?
options: Consumers' spending choices influence what businesses produce
Consumers set prices directly
Consumers own all businesses
Governments decide what is produced
questions.explanation: In a market economy, what people buy signals producers what to make.

questions.stem: What is one reason people work?
options: To avoid paying tax
Only for enjoyment
To earn income to meet needs and wants
Only because it is legally required
questions.explanation: Income is the main reason, though purpose, social connection and status also matter.

questions.stem: A drought reduces wheat harvests. What is the likely effect on wheat prices?
options: Prices rise because supply has fallen while demand is unchanged
Prices fall because there is less wheat
Prices stay the same
Demand falls automatically
questions.explanation: Reduced supply against steady demand pushes prices up.

questions.stem: A new phone becomes very popular. What is the likely effect on its price?
options: Supply falls automatically
Price tends to rise as demand increases
Price falls as demand increases
Price is unaffected by demand
questions.explanation: Rising demand against limited supply pushes prices up, at least in the short term.

questions.stem: Why must a business consider its target market?
options: Target markets are set by government
It determines the tax rate
Products and marketing must suit the customers it hopes to sell to
All customers want the same thing
questions.explanation: Understanding who will buy shapes product design, pricing and promotion.

questions.stem: Which is a legal right of Australian consumers?
options: The right to set the price
The right to take goods without paying if faulty
Goods must be of acceptable quality and match their description
The right to return any item at any time for any reason
questions.explanation: Consumer guarantees cover quality and description. A change-of-mind return is a shop's policy, not a legal right.

questions.stem: Which is a warning sign of a financial scam?
options: The ability to compare prices
Urgent pressure to pay immediately using an unusual payment method
A written receipt provided
A well-known company name on a shopfront
questions.explanation: Urgency plus unusual payment methods are classic indicators, because both make recovery difficult.

questions.stem: Why is a budget useful for achieving a savings goal?
options: It increases income automatically
It removes the need to earn money
It guarantees the goal is reached
It shows whether planned spending leaves enough to save regularly
questions.explanation: Budgets make the gap between income and spending visible so it can be managed.

questions.stem: What is one predicted change in the future of work in Australia?
options: Increased automation changing the tasks in many jobs
A shift of most employment into manufacturing
A steady fall in the number of people seeking work
Fewer people working across more industries
questions.explanation: Automation is expected to reshape roles rather than eliminate work entirely, with demand shifting between skills.

questions.stem: Why do businesses have different goals beyond profit?
options: Profit is set by government for each industry
Businesses adopt other goals only once profitable
Non-profit goals are required of larger businesses
They may pursue social, environmental or community objectives as well
questions.explanation: Social enterprises and not-for-profits are explicit examples; many commercial businesses also set sustainability goals.

questions.stem: A business faces rising costs but cannot raise prices. What is the likely effect?
options: Profit falls unless costs are reduced elsewhere
Profit rises
Revenue automatically increases
Demand automatically increases
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue minus costs, so rising costs with fixed revenue squeeze it.

questions.stem: Why might a person choose self-employment over a wage job?
options: Steadier income and predictable hours, in exchange for less say over the work itself
Lower tax on the same earnings, because business income is assessed at a reduced rate
Shorter working weeks on average, since there is no employer setting required hours
Greater independence and potential returns, accepting greater risk and less security
questions.explanation: The trade-off is autonomy and upside against income variability and risk.

questions.stem: What is the role of incentives in economic decision-making?
options: They remove the need to choose
They only apply to businesses
They eliminate scarcity
They encourage particular choices by changing costs or benefits
questions.explanation: A discount, a tax or a subsidy all work by altering the incentive to act.

questions.stem: Why can a graph of price over time be misleading without context?
options: It may ignore inflation, changes in quality, or a shortened axis that exaggerates change
Graphs are never useful
Price data is always inaccurate
Graphs cannot show trends
questions.explanation: Interpreting graphs critically is an explicit economics skill. Axis choices and missing adjustments both distort the story.

questions.stem: Why might two people make different decisions with identical information?
options: One of them must be irrational
Economic decisions have one correct answer
Information determines the decision entirely
They value the alternatives differently, so their opportunity costs differ
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost depends on personal preferences, so the same trade-off is weighed differently.

questions.stem: A consumer buys a faulty appliance. What is the strongest first step?
options: Buy a replacement immediately and do nothing else
Contact the manufacturer's competitor
Contact the seller with proof of purchase and request a remedy under consumer guarantees
Post about it on social media
questions.explanation: Consumer law places the obligation on the seller, and a documented request is what triggers it.

questions.stem: Why is an economy described as a system?
options: Each part operates independently
It has no moving parts
Decisions by consumers, businesses and government interact and affect one another
It is controlled by a single decision-maker
questions.explanation: Interdependence is the point: a change in one part propagates through the others.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument that entrepreneurship benefits an economy?
options: New businesses create employment, competition and innovation
All new businesses succeed
Entrepreneurs pay no tax
Entrepreneurship removes risk
questions.explanation: The benefits are real but so is failure — most new businesses do not survive long, which is part of the risk.

questions.stem: What is revenue for a business?
options: The total money received from sales
The money left after costs
The money spent on wages
The tax paid
questions.explanation: Profit is revenue minus costs.
questions.teaching:
Business accounts contain two figures that both sound like earnings, and treating them as the same is the most common error in this topic.

The first is everything coming in from sales over a period, before anything is taken out. Out of that the business still has to pay wages, rent, stock and interest. Whatever survives is the second figure. A business can take a large amount and still fail if its costs are larger, which is why the first figure alone says very little about whether a business is healthy.

questions.stem: What are fixed costs?
options: Costs paid by consumers
Costs that stay the same regardless of output
Costs that change with output
One-off costs only
questions.explanation: Rent is a fixed cost; materials per item are variable.

questions.stem: What are variable costs?
options: Costs paid by government
Costs that change with the amount produced
Costs that change with the price charged
Costs paid annually
questions.explanation: Making more units uses more materials, so material cost varies.

questions.stem: What is a market?
options: The price at which a good is sold
Any arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange
A place where goods are stored before sale
The total number of buyers for a good
questions.explanation: Online marketplaces are markets just as much as a produce market.

questions.stem: What is competition between businesses?
options: A type of tax
Rivalry for customers, which can affect prices and quality
Cooperation to set prices
A government regulation
questions.explanation: Competition tends to push prices down and quality up.

questions.stem: What is saving?
options: Spending on essentials
Borrowing money
Paying tax
Setting aside income rather than spending it
questions.explanation: Saving builds funds for future goals or emergencies.
questions.teaching:
Personal finance uses several terms for what happens to income, and they describe different things.

Spending exchanges income for goods and services now. Setting income aside instead, rather than using it, builds a reserve for later — for an emergency, a planned purchase, or retirement. Investing goes a step further, putting money into something expected to grow, which involves risk. Borrowing is the reverse of all of these. The distinction being tested here is between using income now and holding it back.

questions.stem: What is interest on a savings account?
options: A tax on savings
The account balance
Money paid to you for keeping funds with the institution
A fee you pay the bank
questions.explanation: On a loan, interest is what you pay instead.

questions.stem: What is a good compared with a service?
options: A good is a physical item; a service is work performed for someone
They are the same
A good is intangible
A service is always free
questions.explanation: A haircut is a service; the scissors are a good.

questions.stem: What is GST in Australia?
options: A tax on income only
A tax on businesses only
A payment from government
A goods and services tax added to most purchases
questions.explanation: GST is a consumption tax currently levied at 10 per cent.

questions.stem: What is a receipt useful for?
options: Setting a budget only
Proving a purchase was made, which supports consumer rights claims
Increasing the price
Paying tax
questions.explanation: Proof of purchase is generally needed to claim a remedy.

questions.stem: A cafe's rent rises but sales stay the same. What happens to profit?
options: Profit rises
Revenue falls
Profit stays the same because rent is a fixed cost
Profit falls
questions.explanation: Costs rose while revenue was unchanged, so the difference between them shrinks.

questions.stem: A student saves $15 a week towards a $240 item. How long will it take?
options: 12 weeks
20 weeks
24 weeks
16 weeks
questions.explanation: 240 divided by 15 gives 16 weeks.

questions.stem: Why is an emergency fund part of good financial planning?
options: It earns interest that covers small emergencies
It replaces the need for insurance
It protects savings from inflation
It covers unexpected costs without needing to borrow
questions.explanation: An emergency fund is money already set aside, so an unexpected bill is paid from savings rather than from credit. Without one, the same bill becomes debt with interest.

questions.stem: What is the opportunity cost of spending savings on a holiday?
options: Nothing, since it is your money
Whatever else that money could have been used for
The cost of the holiday only
The tax paid
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost applies to every choice, including enjoyable ones.

questions.stem: Why do businesses research their target market?
options: To match products, pricing and promotion to likely customers
Because it is legally required
To set the tax rate
To reduce competition
questions.explanation: Understanding customers reduces the risk of producing something nobody wants.

questions.stem: An online offer asks for payment in gift cards. What should you conclude?
options: This is a strong indicator of a scam
It is a normal payment method
It means the seller is efficient
It guarantees a discount
questions.explanation: Gift card payments are untraceable and unrecoverable, which is exactly why scammers request them.

questions.stem: How does an increase in the number of suppliers usually affect price?
options: Price is unaffected
Demand falls automatically
Increased competition tends to push prices down
Prices always rise
questions.explanation: More supply at a given price, plus competitive pressure, tends to lower prices.

questions.stem: Why do governments regulate consumer guarantees?
options: To increase business profits
Because businesses request it
To raise tax revenue
Individual consumers have less information and power than businesses
questions.explanation: The imbalance in information and bargaining power is the standard justification.

questions.stem: What is one reason the nature of work is changing in Australia?
options: People no longer need income
Businesses have stopped hiring
Education is no longer relevant
Technology is automating routine tasks and creating new roles
questions.explanation: Automation shifts the mix of skills demanded rather than removing work altogether.

questions.stem: Why does a market price tend to settle where supply and demand meet?
options: Producers agree a price in advance and buyers accept it for want of an alternative
Above it there is unsold surplus; below it there is unmet demand, and both push price towards balance
The government sets a target and adjusts taxes until the market settles there
Prices drift upward until buyers stop purchasing and the market resets itself
questions.explanation: Surplus and shortage each create pressure in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A business claims a product is 'the best available'. What should a consumer consider?
options: That price alone determines quality
Whether the claim is substantiated and whether the seller benefits from making it
That the claim must be true
That all such claims are illegal
questions.explanation: Evaluating claims against evidence and interest is the core consumer skill.

questions.stem: Why can a low price be a poor guide to value?
options: Durability, running costs and quality affect total cost over time
Low prices are always a scam
A low price signals the seller is making a loss
Expensive is always better
questions.explanation: A cheap item replaced three times may cost more than one durable purchase.

questions.stem: Which best explains why entrepreneurship carries risk?
options: New businesses cannot borrow
Risk is imaginary
Costs are incurred before revenue is certain, and demand may not eventuate
Entrepreneurs pay more tax
questions.explanation: Upfront investment against uncertain demand is the essential risk.

questions.stem: Why should a graph of business profit be examined for its time period?
options: Graphs cannot show profit
A short period can hide seasonal patterns or a longer-term trend
A longer period always shows steadier profit
Longer periods are always misleading
questions.explanation: Selecting a favourable window is a common way of presenting data misleadingly.

questions.stem: What is a consumer's main role in an economy?
options: Manufacturing goods
Setting tax rates
Employing workers
Buying goods and services, which signals what should be produced
questions.explanation: Consumer spending guides producers through consumer sovereignty.

questions.stem: What is a producer?
options: A bank customer
A person or business that makes goods or provides services
Someone who buys goods
A government regulator
questions.explanation: Producers combine resources to create output.

questions.stem: What are economic resources?
options: Only natural materials
Only workers
Inputs such as land, labour, capital and enterprise used to produce goods
Only money
questions.explanation: The four factors of production are the standard categorisation.

questions.stem: What is capital in economics?
options: Natural resources
The workforce
Equipment and tools used to produce goods and services
Money in a bank only
questions.explanation: Machinery and buildings are capital; money is a means of acquiring it.
questions.teaching:
Economists group the inputs used to produce anything into a small number of categories.

Land covers natural resources. Labour covers human effort and skill. Enterprise covers the organising and risk-taking that brings the others together. And one category covers the produced goods used to make other goods — machinery, tools, buildings, vehicles, computers. The distinguishing feature is that these were themselves produced and are then used in further production rather than consumed directly.

questions.stem: What is a franchise?
options: A sole trader
A government business
A charity
A business operating under an established brand and system by agreement
questions.explanation: The franchisee pays for the right to use the brand and model.
questions.teaching:
Businesses are structured in several ways, and each involves a different relationship between the owner and the brand.

A sole trader owns and runs everything. A partnership shares that between people. A company is a separate legal entity. And one arrangement lets an operator run their own business using an established brand, products and systems under licence, paying fees for the right. The operator gets a proven model and instant recognition; the trade-off is limited freedom and ongoing payments to the brand owner.

questions.stem: What is a not-for-profit organisation?
options: One that pays no wages
A government department
One that reinvests any surplus into its purpose rather than distributing profit
One that makes no money
questions.explanation: Not-for-profits can and do generate revenue; they just do not distribute profit to owners.

questions.stem: What is a salary?
options: A fixed annual amount paid for a role, usually in regular instalments
Payment per hour worked
Payment per item produced
A one-off payment
questions.explanation: Wages are typically hourly; salaries are annual.

questions.stem: What is superannuation in Australia?
options: A type of tax refund
A bank loan
A weekly wage
Money set aside during working life to fund retirement
questions.explanation: Employers are generally required to contribute a percentage of earnings.
questions.teaching:
Australia funds retirement partly through a compulsory saving system built up during working life.

Employers must pay a set percentage of an employee's ordinary earnings into a fund, on top of wages, under the Superannuation Guarantee introduced in 1992. That money is invested and generally cannot be touched until retirement age, and it receives concessional tax treatment which is why it grows faster than ordinary savings. It remains the worker's own money throughout, which is what distinguishes it from a tax.

questions.stem: What is a warranty?
options: A receipt
A price tag
A type of tax
A promise by a seller or maker to repair or replace faulty goods
questions.explanation: Warranties are in addition to consumer guarantees under the law.
questions.teaching:
Consumers have several protections when something goes wrong, and they come from different places.

Australian Consumer Law gives automatic guarantees that apply whether or not anything was promised — goods must be of acceptable quality and fit for purpose. Separately, a seller or manufacturer may offer their own promise to repair, replace or refund within a set period. That voluntary promise is what this question is about, and the important point is that it sits on top of the legal guarantees rather than replacing them.

questions.stem: What is inflation?
options: A fall in prices
An increase in wages only
A type of tax
A general rise in prices over time
questions.explanation: Inflation reduces what a given amount of money can buy.
questions.teaching:
Individual prices move constantly for their own reasons. This term describes something broader: a sustained rise in the general price level across the economy.

In Australia it is measured through the Consumer Price Index, which tracks a fixed basket of household goods and services. The consequence is about money rather than goods: if everything costs more, each dollar buys less, so the purchasing power of money falls as the figure rises. The two move in opposite directions, which is the point most often reversed. The Reserve Bank targets 2–3% on average, since mild inflation is considered healthier than prices falling.

questions.stem: Why does inflation matter to someone with savings?
options: Money kept as cash buys less over time as prices rise
Interest always rises faster than prices do
Inflation affects spending but not money already saved
Savings lose value only if withdrawn during inflation
questions.explanation: Interest below the inflation rate means real value is falling.

questions.stem: A business faces new competition. What is a likely response?
options: Raising prices to signal higher quality than the rival
Reducing stock until the competitor establishes itself
Waiting for the competitor to set its prices first
Lowering prices, improving quality or differentiating its product
questions.explanation: Competition pressures businesses to improve their offer.

questions.stem: Why do governments regulate advertising claims?
options: To reduce competition
Advertising is not regulated
To prevent consumers being misled into purchases
To increase business revenue
questions.explanation: Misleading conduct provisions protect the information consumers rely on.

questions.stem: Why is comparing unit prices useful when shopping?
options: It shows the total cost only
It reveals the brand
It is required by law
It allows different package sizes to be compared fairly
questions.explanation: Price per 100 g or per litre is the standard comparison basis.

questions.stem: How does entrepreneurship contribute to employment?
options: New businesses mostly replace jobs lost elsewhere
New businesses create jobs as they grow
Entrepreneurs hire only after several profitable years
Employment depends on population rather than new firms
questions.explanation: Small and new businesses account for a substantial share of job creation.

questions.stem: Why do people with the same income sometimes have very different savings?
options: Savings rise automatically as income rises
Savings depend mainly on how often someone is paid
Spending choices, fixed costs and financial planning differ
Savings are set by the interest rate on the account
questions.explanation: Budgeting and priorities shape outcomes as much as income does.

questions.stem: Why can a subsidy for one industry impose costs on the wider economy?
options: Funds come from taxation and may support less efficient production
Subsidies raise prices for consumers in that industry
Subsidies transfer costs from producers to importers
Subsidies are repaid by the industry over time
questions.explanation: Weighing benefits against costs, including who bears them, is the required analysis.

questions.stem: Why does predicting the future of work involve uncertainty?
options: Technological, economic and social changes interact in ways that are hard to forecast
Predictions are always accurate
The future of work is fixed
Only technology matters
questions.explanation: Forecasts are useful for planning but should be treated as scenarios rather than certainties.
